title: Health, Safety and Security in Kenyan Schools (2026 Guide)
h1: Health, Safety and Security in Kenyan Schools (2026 Guide)
description: Health, safety and security in Kenyan schools — clinics and health records, safe buildings and water, food safety, access control and emergency planning.
author: SQUL Team
intro: Nothing else matters if learners are not safe. Health, safety and security are the foundation a school's reputation rests on, and they are largely a matter of routine rather than heroics. This guide covers **health, safety and security in Kenyan schools**, part of our wider guide on [how to manage a school in Kenya](/blog/how-to-manage-a-school-in-kenya).
It is general guidance, not legal advice — confirm current requirements with the relevant authorities.

items: **A workable clinic** with basic supplies and a clear referral route to local facilities.
**Health notes per learner** accessible to the right staff, especially for boarders.
**A clinic log** of visits and treatments, kept confidential.
**Emergency contacts** for each learner, current and reachable.

rows: Sound structures; maintenance planned, not reactive
Safe, adequate supply; tanks cleaned and covered
Clean, adequate and separated for learners
Exits clear; extinguishers present and in date
Safe play areas; hazards removed or fenced

blocks.title: Routine, not reaction
blocks.text: Safety failures are usually maintenance failures. A scheduled walk-round each term catches most of them before an inspector does.

For boarding schools, the kitchen is a daily risk. Keep it clean, supervise handlers, store food properly, and keep records. Food that makes learners ill closes a school faster than almost anything else.

items: **One controlled entrance** where visitors are registered.
**Visitor policy** — sign in, badge, and be accompanied.
**Adequate supervision** in corridors, dorms and grounds.
**Clear procedures** for a learner leaving school early.

sections.heading: An emergency plan you have practised

items.title: Define the likely emergencies
items.text: Fire, medical, severe weather, intruder, utilities failure.

items.title: Assign roles
items.text: Who calls, who assembles learners, who contacts parents.

items.title: Communicate to parents
items.text: A short, factual message over WhatsApp and SMS beats rumour.

items.title: Practise and review
items.text: A drill each term, and a review of what went wrong.

items: **Stale emergency contacts** — a parent who cannot be reached in a crisis.
**Health notes locked away** from the staff who need them in an emergency.

faqs.question: What safety and security does a Kenyan school need?
faqs.answer: Safe, maintained buildings and water, clean sanitation, working fire provisions, controlled access with visitor registration, adequate supervision, and a practised emergency plan. Confirm current requirements with the relevant authorities.

faqs.question: Why keep a clinic log in schools?
faqs.answer: A confidential clinic log tracks visits and treatments, helps spot patterns (like a spreading illness), and supports emergency responses. Health notes per learner should be accessible to the right staff.

faqs.question: How should schools communicate during an emergency?
faqs.answer: Send a short, factual message to parents over WhatsApp and SMS as soon as the situation is under control — silence invites rumour and panic.

faqs.question: How often should a school run emergency drills?
faqs.answer: At least once a term, with a review afterwards. A drill nobody practises is not a plan.
